description: Why countries trade, how UK imports and exports work, and how exchange rates affect prices.
content_html:
Why Countries Trade

No country produces everything its people want. The UK cannot grow coffee, mine significant quantities of oil, or manufacture every component inside a smartphone — so it buys these from other countries. At the same time, the UK sells financial services, pharmaceuticals, aerospace equipment and creative content to the rest of the world. This two-way flow of goods and services is international trade.

Countries trade because of comparative advantage: a country should focus on producing goods where its relative opportunity cost is lowest, rather than the goods it simply makes cheapest in absolute terms. Even if one country is more efficient at producing everything, trade still benefits both sides, because each can concentrate on what it does at the lowest relative cost. Countries then export these specialised goods and import those where a trading partner has the comparative advantage — and both end up with more than if they each tried to be self-sufficient.

Key Fact

The UK’s main exports include financial and professional services, pharmaceuticals, aerospace and motor vehicles. Its main imports include manufactured goods, fuels, foodstuffs and electronic components. The UK typically imports more goods than it exports — running a deficit on trade in goods — but earns a surplus on trade in services.

Imports, Exports and the Balance of Trade

Exports bring money into an economy: when a UK car manufacturer sells vehicles to Germany, foreign currency flows into the UK. Imports send money out: when a UK consumer buys an American streaming subscription or a Japanese games console, pounds leave the UK economy. The difference between the value of exports and the value of imports is the balance of trade.

If exports exceed imports, the country has a trade surplus. If imports exceed exports, it has a trade deficit. A persistent deficit can be a concern for the government: it means the country is spending more on foreign goods than it earns from selling abroad, which may put downward pressure on the currency and affect domestic jobs in industries that compete with cheap imports.

Imagine the UK earns £500 billion from exports in a year but spends £600 billion on imports. That £100 billion shortfall is a trade deficit. To fill the gap, the UK must attract foreign money in other ways — for example, by selling assets, borrowing from abroad, or earning income from overseas investments. A surplus country (say, Germany from its car and machine exports) takes in more than it pays out, building up foreign currency reserves or overseas investments. Neither position is automatically good or bad: a deficit can reflect a strong consumer economy, while a surplus can reflect weak domestic demand.

What Is an Exchange Rate?

To trade internationally you need to convert currencies. An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another. For example, if the exchange rate between the pound and the dollar is £1 = $1.25, you can swap one pound for one dollar and twenty-five cents. Exchange rates change constantly because they are determined by the demand for and supply of currencies on the foreign exchange market, which operates twenty-four hours a day.

Key Fact

Two acronyms help you remember the effects of exchange rate changes. SPICED: a Strong Pound makes Imports Cheap but Exports Dear (harder to sell abroad). WPIDEC: a Weak Pound makes Imports Dear but Exports Cheap (easier to sell abroad). Learning both acronyms together prevents mixing them up.

How Exchange Rates Are Determined

Think of currency like any other good: if demand for pounds rises, the price of pounds (the exchange rate) rises too. Demand for pounds increases when foreigners want to buy British goods and services, invest in UK assets, or benefit from higher UK interest rates. Supply of pounds increases when UK residents want to buy foreign goods or invest overseas — they sell pounds to get other currencies.

When demand for the pound rises relative to its supply — perhaps because the Bank of England raises interest rates, attracting foreign investors who must first buy pounds — the exchange rate rises. This is called appreciation. When demand falls or supply rises, the exchange rate falls. This is called depreciation.

To picture appreciation: imagine a demand and supply diagram for pounds. The horizontal axis shows the quantity of pounds traded; the vertical axis shows the exchange rate expressed as dollars per pound ($/£) — how many dollars one pound buys. If UK interest rates rise, demand for pounds shifts to the right. The new equilibrium exchange rate is higher — the pound has appreciated. The opposite shift (demand falling) gives a lower equilibrium — depreciation.

Students frequently confuse appreciation and depreciation. A simple check: if £1 buys more dollars today than yesterday, the pound has appreciated (gone up in value). If £1 buys fewer dollars, it has depreciated (gone down). Appreciation and depreciation are the terms used when exchange rates are set by the market. The equivalent terms when a government pegs its currency and adjusts it deliberately are revaluation (up) and devaluation (down) — you may encounter these in extended-answer questions.

Effects of Exchange Rate Changes on Exporters, Importers and Consumers

Exchange rate changes ripple through the economy in predictable chains. Work through SPICED and WPIDEC for each scenario.

The pound appreciates (rises in value): a UK exporter selling machinery priced in pounds suddenly looks more expensive to a foreign buyer who must convert their currency into pounds. Demand for UK exports may fall — particularly if the exporter’s goods are price-elastic. UK importers benefit: foreign goods cost fewer pounds to buy, so UK firms importing raw materials or components face lower costs. Consumers see cheaper foreign goods on the shelves, which keeps inflation down. However, domestic industries facing cheaper foreign competition may lose sales and jobs.

The pound depreciates (falls in value): exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, which can boost demand for British goods and help UK firms win market share abroad. This follows the chain: depreciation → lower export prices in foreign currency → higher foreign demand → more UK production → possible jobs boost. The downside is that imports become more expensive. Raw material costs for UK manufacturers rise, pushing up the cost of production. Consumers face higher prices for imported food, fuel and electronics — feeding through to inflation. The Bank of England watches currency movements closely because a sharp depreciation can push inflation above its 2% target.
exam_tip_html: Exchange rate questions reward clear chains of reasoning. The command word “Explain” means you must develop the point: don’t just write “a weaker pound makes exports cheaper” — follow it with “because foreign buyers need fewer units of their own currency to buy the same British good, so demand for UK exports rises.” For “Analyse” and “Evaluate” questions, remember that the size of the effect depends on price elasticity: if export demand is inelastic (buyers have few alternatives), a depreciation will not boost revenue much. Always use the SPICED/WPIDEC mnemonics to anchor your answer, and name a specific group affected (UK car manufacturer, UK consumer, UK importer of food).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Countries trade because no single country is efficient at producing everything — specialising and trading raises total output. The UK runs a surplus on trade in services but a deficit on trade in goods.
  • Exchange rates are determined by demand and supply of currencies. A rise in demand for the pound causes appreciation; a fall causes depreciation.
  • SPICED (Strong Pound → Imports Cheap, Exports Dear) and WPIDEC (Weak Pound → Imports Dear, Exports Cheap) capture the core effects. Consumers, exporters and importers are affected in opposite directions when the exchange rate changes.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an exchange rate?
A) The interest rate set by the Bank of England
B) The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency
C) The difference between a country's exports and its imports
D) The tax applied to imported goods
practice_questions.marks: B) The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
The exchange rate between the pound and the euro is £1 = €1.20. A British tourist wants to convert £250 into euros. Calculate how many euros they will receive.
Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: £250 × 1.20 (or €1.20 per £1 × 250); 1 mark for the correct answer of €300.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a depreciation of the pound might benefit UK exporters.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the benefit (e.g. UK goods become cheaper for foreign buyers); 1 mark for developing the chain of reasoning (foreign buyers need less of their own currency to buy the same British good, so demand for UK exports rises); 1 mark for a further consequence or supporting point (e.g. UK exporters may sell more units, increasing their revenue and output).

practice_questions.text:
TechBuild Ltd is a UK manufacturer that imports electronic components from Japan and sells finished products in both the UK and Germany. The pound has recently depreciated against the yen and the euro.
Explain how this depreciation is likely to affect TechBuild Ltd.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a cost effect (components priced in yen now cost more pounds, so production costs rise); 1 mark for developing this (lower profit margins or higher prices charged to customers); 1 mark for identifying a revenue effect (UK goods priced in pounds are now cheaper in euros for German buyers, potentially increasing export demand); 1 mark for developing this (TechBuild may sell more units in Germany or be able to hold euro prices steady and gain market share).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how an appreciation of the pound is likely to affect the UK economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise, connected chain that covers at least two groups (e.g. exporters and consumers/importers), explains the direction and mechanism of each effect, and considers a qualifying factor such as the price elasticity of demand for imports or exports.
Secure: Clear explanation of both the export and import effects with correct direction, using SPICED or equivalent reasoning, though the chain may stop short of a qualifying factor.
Developing: One effect identified and partly developed; the second effect may be stated but not explained; some relevant terms used.
Emerging: A simple correct statement (e.g. ‘exports become more expensive’) with little development; no chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
'A depreciation of the pound always benefits the UK economy.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- UK exporters gain a price advantage in overseas markets; foreign demand for British goods rises, boosting output, employment and firm revenues.
- A weaker pound can stimulate economic growth by raising net exports (exports minus imports), feeding positively into GDP.
- Domestic producers who compete with foreign imports gain market share as imported alternatives become more expensive.

Arguments against:
- Imports become more expensive, raising costs for firms that rely on imported raw materials and components; this can cause cost-push inflation.
- Consumers face higher prices for imported food, fuel and electronics, reducing real incomes and living standards.
- The export boost depends on the price elasticity of demand for UK goods: if overseas buyers have few alternatives (inelastic demand) they may simply pay higher prices in their own currency, but if demand is elastic the gain may not materialise quickly.
- A sharp depreciation can undermine business confidence and reduce inward investment if it signals economic instability.

Judgement: The statement is too absolute. The net effect depends on the state of the economy (an export-led economy benefits more), the elasticity of demand for imports and exports, and how persistent the depreciation is. A moderate depreciation may help growth in the short run, but if it triggers sustained inflation it can harm consumers and workers, particularly those on fixed incomes.

Mastering: Balanced analysis of both sides with developed chains; a supported judgement that evaluates the conditions under which the benefit holds or fails.
Secure: Both sides covered with clear explanation; a judgement is offered but may be less developed.
Developing: One side developed, the other stated; a conclusion present but unsupported.
Emerging: One or two simple points; little balance or judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What does it mean when a currency depreciates?
options: Its value rises against other currencies
Its value falls against other currencies
Interest rates are cut by the central bank

knowledge_checks.q: Which group benefits most directly when the pound appreciates?
options: UK exporters, whose goods become cheaper abroad
UK importers, who can buy foreign goods more cheaply
Workers in export industries, who see rising demand
The government, which collects more tariff revenue

knowledge_checks.q: The difference between the value of a country's exports and the value of its imports is called the _____.
In the SPICED acronym, the letter E stands for Exports becoming _____ when the pound is strong.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: A rise in the value of a currency against other currencies
A fall in the value of a currency against other currencies
The difference between the value of exports and imports

flashcard_questions.a: The buying and selling of goods and services across national borders.
The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.

flashcard_questions.q: What is appreciation of a currency?
flashcard_questions.a: A rise in the currency's value against other currencies in a market-determined system.

flashcard_questions.q: What is depreciation of a currency?
flashcard_questions.a: A fall in the currency's value against other currencies in a market-determined system.

flashcard_questions.q: In SPICED, what does a strong pound do to import prices?
In SPICED, what does a strong pound do to export prices for foreign buyers?
In WPIDEC, what does a weak pound do to import prices?
flashcard_questions.a: Makes imports dearer (more expensive for UK buyers).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the balance of trade?
flashcard_questions.a: The difference between the value of a country's exports and the value of its imports.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might demand for pounds rise on the foreign exchange market?
flashcard_questions.a: Foreigners want to buy UK goods, invest in UK assets, or benefit from higher UK interest rates.

flashcard_questions.q: A depreciation of the pound raises the cost of imported raw materials. What type of inflation can this cause?
What type of trade does the UK typically run a surplus on, even though it runs a deficit on trade in goods?
What is the dollar price for a US buyer if £1 = $1.25 and a UK firm sells a product for £400?
Why does a depreciation boost export demand rather than just export revenue?
flashcard_questions.a: UK goods cost less in foreign currency, so foreign buyers purchase more units.

glossary_terms.definition: The buying and selling of goods and services across national borders.
Goods and services sold by a country to buyers in other countries, bringing money into the domestic economy.
Goods and services bought by a country from producers in other countries, sending money out of the domestic economy.
The difference between the value of a country's exports and the value of its imports.
The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.
A rise in the value of a currency against other currencies in a floating exchange rate system.
A fall in the value of a currency against other currencies in a floating exchange rate system.
